original.target_description: Experiment 3, latency to detect snakes versus caterpillars in 3-year-olds and accompanying parents; target test unresolved between pooled stimulus effect, age-by-target interaction, and age-specific contrast.

notes: Identity assessment: supplied canonical text is the primary Research Article "Detecting the Snake in the Grass", subtitle "Attention to Fear-Relevant Stimuli by Adults and Young Children", by Vanessa LoBue and Judy S. DeLoache, University of Virginia. Psychological Science, Volume 19, Number 3, pages 284–289, copyright 2008, matches the neutral reference. Full six-page article text includes methods, Experiments 1–3, discussion, references, and received/revision dates. DOI is not printed in this text; DOI identity cannot be independently checked from the permitted source. No PDF path supplied, so no PDF rendered. Study 3 and source page 5 (printed p. 288) are identified, but the neutral description does not specify the pooled target-stimulus main effect, age-by-target interaction, or child/adult simple contrast. Both the target-stimulus main effect and age-by-target interaction directly concern the described snake-detection outcome; selecting between them would require an additional test locator. Candidate printed tests: target-stimulus main effect F(1, 44) = 13.42, p < .01; age-by-target interaction F(1, 44) = 5.12, p < .05. The age main effect F(1, 44) = 29.05, p < .01 and snake-experience effect F(1, 44) = 0.16, p = .69 are also printed but do not directly test the snake-versus-caterpillar detection contrast. Child-only snake advantage is described as significant, without a separate printed F/p. No candidate is promoted to a verified assigned statistic. Candidate documented participant N for the full Experiment 3 model: 24 children + 24 parents = 48 distinct participants across mutually exclusive age groups; not 48 independent families. Candidate child-only N = 24. Three additional children were excluded for failure to follow directions (1 snake-target, 2 caterpillar-target); these are not added to the final group counts. The source does not say whether these excluded children had parents tested. General Analyses, p. 286, states that only correct-target trials were included; p. 286 continuation says fewer than 5% of trials were errors in Experiments 2 and 3. These are trial exclusions, not additional documented participant exclusions. N is not inferred from degrees of freedom. Because test correspondence remains unresolved, model N is retained only as candidate evidence for parent field-scope review. Only assigned unfinished fields were assessed. Unassigned fields/sides are null placeholders and must not overwrite prior verified fields.
